title: Derryloran & Cookstown
standfirst: The Gortin and Mitchell-family branches now enter the existing older Tyrone/Corvanaghan working model through two uncertain fathers. The Hillsdale core is separately probable; conflicting child groups, ages and origins remain explicit.
question: Can later Cookstown profiles be matched to a specific 1740 householder?
answer: The Cookstown–Gortin review selects two uncertain father links while retaining the competing identities and no new mothers. The named Hillsdale core is probable. Working update, 16 October 2026: the Corvanaghan James is provisionally identified with the Moneymore James and placed under the latter’s already uncertain older James father. This inherits uncertainty in both identity and pedigree; it does not establish a mother or migration. The 1759 Drumcarn will identity and Mitchell-family alternative remain unresolved. The returns firmly establish a Glasgow population in Derryloran, but they give no ages, spouses, children or relationships. The later James and William profiles remain leads within the wider Tyrone setting, not identified 1740 householders. 20 October 2026: Killycurragh gains a selected possible Kirknewton connection at 36%, and James-1025’s existing father is reassessed to 32%. The minister’s Irish father is 94% and Margaret’s is 84%; the Scottish identities remain unproved. See the linked Killycurragh generations review.

chapters.title: Killycorragh to Ohio: the Glendinning household
body: Research rationale: test the eight-child Killycorragh household against its actual cited family publication, while separating the named children from their later adult identifications.

The visually checked 1903 family memorial, PDF p.17, explicitly names William Glasgow of Killycorragh and Nancy Glendinning as parents of five sons, Henry Cunningham, Adam, Isaac Watts, Benjamin and Alexander Flemming, and three daughters, Mary, Matilda and Jane. Nancy’s reported April 1803 birth and 20 March 1890 Belle Center death anchor this particular family.

Mary Glasgow: 88% → 97%. Mary represents the named daughter in the family account itself; there is no separately claimed later adult identity to bridge. Her circa-1824 birth remains an estimate, not a birth date supplied by this book.

Matilda (Glasgow) Ewing: 83% → 92%. The named daughter Matilda and the existing 22 December 1854 Sandusky marriage to James Ewing fit William’s specific Sandusky household before his 1855 death. The book does not name her husband, so that adult identification still combines sources.

Alexander Fleming Glasgow: 85% → 95%. The distinctive Alexander Fleming matches the book’s Alexander Flemming, with the existing Irish origin and Belle Center sibling context. This is a specific family identification rather than a shared first name alone.

Benjamin Glasgow: 84% → 88%. The book establishes a son Benjamin in this exact family. Connecting him to the 1841–1916 Northwood adult still depends on the existing family attribution and sibling setting; no literal adult parent inscription has been inspected.

Jane Glasgow: 82% → 86%. The book establishes a daughter Jane in this exact family. Identification with the 1828–1903 memorial remains less secure because no held spouse, parental inscription or explicit adult sibling clause bridges them.

This is a retrospective family publication, not an original baptism register. Earlier WikiTree Space citations derive from the same publication and are not independent witnesses. The list gives no dates or spouses for the children and does not establish an interleaved birth order. Each percentage concerns the specific father-profile pair, with later adult identity assessed separately. William’s own father remains unknown and unrated; Adam-3151 remains 77% probable because the 1834/1840 birth claims and Arthur’s Ohio-born son Adam-2387 are unresolved. Henry Cunningham-3148 and Isaac Watts-3149 remain 92%. No maternal assessment, structured vital field, selected father ID or live WikiTree flag is changed.

Next questions: trace the father of William of Killycorragh through local land/church records; resolve Adam’s rival adult identity before any merge. The London/Hull physician in the T1959 letter is not identified with this Ohio ruling elder.

chapters.period: c.1730–1848 · uncertain branch joins; named core probable
chapters.title: Cookstown and Gortin: two working links for 23 detached profiles
body: Select the older James Glasgow-1025 account as the Cookstown progenitor James Glasgow-1970’s uncertain working father, conditional on the existing Corvanaghan/Moneymore family model. The c.1700 and c.1730 estimates allow a father–son generation. James-1970 is already a surviving possible identity for the Cookstown-area Corvanaghan James-2988, whose selected working father is James-1025 through the separate Moneymore comparison. Extending that same unproved pedigree gives the Mitchell account a consistent, revisable place in the broader family. The district context comes from those Cookstown/Corvanaghan/Moneymore comparisons, not from the 1759 index. This is an inherited family hypothesis with no independent father record for the Mitchell progenitor.

No will, lease or baptism names the Cookstown James as the older James’s son. The reviewed PRONI detail says Drumcarn, County Tyrone, not Drumearn, and gives 17 January 1759 without age or kin; the modern profile identity and meaning of that date remain unresolved. It cannot corroborate Drumearn residence, a death date, or this father choice. The older and younger James accounts may themselves be duplicates rather than separate generations; if established, the father edge must collapse. The existing older pedigree and the Corvanaghan/Moneymore identity remain unproved. The 1879 history reports Scotland-to-Cookstown migration about 1750, while the older James’s profile is placed in Tyrone; neither a return journey nor that Scottish birthplace is established here. Multiple James and William householders appear in the 1740 Derryloran return, and two James men appear at Drumearn in 1766. William or another local father, a collateral link and a separate Scottish origin remain alternatives. Mary Harkness is not transferred to the Mitchell account, and Margaret Rutherford is not assigned as its mother. James-1970, James-2988, James-1024 and the older James-1025 remain separate possible overlapping reconstructions, not independently proved sons or households.

Assess the Hillsdale record-defined core as probable: James Glasgow-1970 as John Glasgow-1968’s father, Unknown Mitchell as that John’s mother, and James and Mitchell as spouses. The 1879 account explicitly gives those relationships; the 1888 sketches identify the same John–Jane household through sons William and John, their seven-child group and Michigan history. These are detailed late family accounts, not contemporary Scottish or Irish birth/marriage entries. Conflicting Scottish versus Tyrone origins, c.1778 dating and 1844/1848 immigration years limit the life-history reconstruction. The family-role identification is still a justified probable inference, while exact dates and the new upstream/Gortin links remain weaker separate questions. The prior local grades were unknown with saved unmarked parent flags; no already-confident link is counted as a new upgrade.

Select James Glasgow-1970 of the Cookstown Mitchell family as John Glasgow-2539 of Gortin’s uncertain working father, through the existing possible identification with John Glasgow-1968. The 1879 Hillsdale history specifically identifies James and his Mitchell wife as parents of John, a farmer near Cookstown. The Gortin account supplies another John in the same Derryloran/Cookstown locality and an earlier compatible father generation. The maintained Hillsdale research already lists Gortin John as a possible duplicate. This is a positive named-son comparison in the relevant family and locality, stronger than an arbitrary father chosen only from the surname. Prefer this existing family as a revisable home for the 17-profile Gortin branch; retain both John accounts separately.

The identity is uncertain. The Hillsdale histories describe John and Jane’s seven children as Robert, Mary A., William, John, Bessie, James and Margaret; the Gortin account instead links Francis, Hugh, Letitia and Samuel. No child has been matched across those sets. An earlier union could explain different couple-based lists, but none is established here and no additional marriage is invented. If the seven-child account was intended as an exhaustive lifetime list for John, the extra Gortin group would conflict with it. The Gortin before-1771 birth boundary comes from Samuel’s reported 1792 birth; the Hillsdale c.1778 father estimate is younger. Literal 1778 fatherhood of a 1792 child would be about 14 and is a serious constraint. These are reconstructed ages and estimates, not two original birth entries; both are retained, without silently shifting either date. Sarah MacNeece’s status as the Gortin man’s widow and Jane’s identity also require testing; no mother is transferred to Gortin John and no wife is added or replaced. Another local John, a collateral relationship, or different father remain alternatives. The 1700s and 1800s family accounts do not independently prove these two Johns identical.

Two uncertain working father links join the previously detached 6-profile Cookstown family and 17-profile Gortin family to the main working tree. The 23 are retained pre-1850 profile accounts, including unresolved possible duplicates, not 23 newly discovered or independently verified people. Motherhood and marriage grades apply only to the named Hillsdale core; no mother, spouse, birth/death change, new person or merge is added elsewhere. All raw WikiTree family fields remain intact and no live save is made. The working connectivity gain measures selected hypotheses, while confidently marked connectivity remains unchanged. This batch reuses maintained source reviews and makes no new original-page inspection claim. Complete private comparisons stay off the public site where they contain living-person or DNA material; safe conclusions and parent choices remain visible.

The full T1959/3 family-letter transcription, read on 20 October 2026, distinguishes the older Killycurragh William from his son William, husband of Miss Cunningham. The younger William is the selected father of Rev. John of New Row, Coleraine, at 94%; Margaret, John’s wife, is placed under William Glasgow-2426 at 84%. The new 36% father proposal from the Cunningham husband to William Glasgow-1318 joins this household to the existing Scottish working family. The letter supplies the Irish generations; the Scottish child’s adult identity and migration remain unproved. The John of Gortin and John of Coleraine are separate generations and accounts.

chapters.title: Corvanaghan and Moneymore: a conditional James family
body: Glasgow-1025 is selected as the very uncertain working father of Glasgow-2988, the 1766 Corvanaghan householder, through preferred provisional identity with Glasgow-1024 of Moneymore. The existing Corvanaghan biography already retains the Moneymore man as a compatible candidate: the places are roughly nine miles apart, the name matches and their circa 1720/1722 births are estimates rather than a real two-year conflict. The 1766 Irish occurrence can precede the compiled 1770 immigration claim associated with the Moneymore family; no post 1766 Irish occurrence has been assigned to the Corvanaghan man. This is a weak locality and chronology preference, not proof of emigration or identity. The older James is already an uncertain father in the Moneymore pedigree. Extending that attachment gives the Corvanaghan account a conditional place in the same family, without inventing an intermediate generation. It inherits two major uncertainties: adult identity and the older pedigree itself.

The older James account’s circa 1700 birth would allow an ordinary father–son interval of about 20–22 years, if the estimates are close. Those guessed years do not independently establish paternity. No contemporary record names the older James as father of either Moneymore James or the Corvanaghan householder. The current older-father attachment is a tree hypothesis, not a clause in the 1766 return, the pension record or the later family history. The older and younger James accounts might themselves be duplicates rather than father and son; if that identity is established, this additional father edge must collapse with it. Their existing Scottish ancestral attachments receive no new support. No mother is selected: the uncertain Rutherford attachment on the Moneymore account is not independently supported for the Corvanaghan man and is not copied.

The 1766 Kildress return names James Glasgow as a Protestant householder at Corvanaghan. It gives no age, birthplace, wife, children, occupation or father. The two sons currently attached as Glasgow-2989 and Glasgow-2990 remain unproved, with their existing grades and dates unchanged. Their estimated generations cannot identify the householder. Corvanaghan is distinct from Gortnavreeghan in County Cavan; the rejected Cavan lease assignment is not restored. The 1740 Derryloran return contains two James and two William householders without townlands or kinship, and the 1766 Derryloran return separately names two Jas. Glasgo at Drumearn. None is newly assigned to a particular generation.

Faris’s later genealogy calls Glasgow-12’s father James of Moneymore, but the underlying evidence for that father identification has not been inspected. Robert’s 1834 pension declaration gives County Derry birth in 1749 and arrival in Virginia in 1769; it does not name parents or siblings. The fuller Mary Harkness and sibling package, the compiled 1770 entry and the 1804 same-name naturalisation applicant remain separate inherited claims. The reported departure of a mother and elder brothers by 1766 does not independently place their father in America that year. No new wife, emigrant child, ship, naturalisation identity or extreme-age death is attached to the Corvanaghan account. The 1766 return and the later Moneymore family tradition may still concern different men.

Glasgow-1970 of the Mitchell-family tradition remains a live alternative identity for the Corvanaghan householder. The 1879 Hillsdale history describes a Scotsman and his Mitchell wife moving to the Cookstown area about 1750, with a son John and later Michigan descendants. It does not name Corvanaghan. The Moneymore route is preferred only weakly for its more specific nearby locality and compatible 1766 window; the Mitchell account is not excluded, and the birthplaces on the compared profiles are not independent proof. Another local James remains possible. The absence of Glasgow occupiers at Corvanaghan in the 1826 tithe list, sixty years later, does not establish death or emigration.

The 1759 will reference does not prove this father generation. The previously reviewed PRONI detail names Drumcarn, not Drumearn, and supplies no age or kin. It may concern the older account, the Moneymore James or another namesake. The meaning of 17 January 1759 and the testator’s modern profile identity remain unresolved. No 1759 death, estate event or residence is transferred to the 1766 Corvanaghan householder. The older profile’s structured dates and places are retained as existing fields with those qualifications; the new parent model does not resolve them.

One very uncertain father is newly selected through a possible Moneymore identity and an already uncertain older pedigree. No mother, source-proved parentage, migration, merge, vital-field change, original inspection, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. The compared James accounts remain separate and may be duplicates rather than distinct brothers or generations. Working connectivity counts retained accounts and does not independently validate those identities. Full comparisons containing living-person references remain private; the historical findings and relationships remain public.

23 October 2026 actual-book boundary: Existing father-profile propositions only: Robert-12 85% → 35%; Arthur-649 and Joseph-1543 each 82% → 35%; John-4027 76% → 30%; Mary-4030 64% → 22%. All five were probable; the first four are now possible and Mary uncertain. James-1024 remains the selected named candidate; no attachment is removed. James-1024’s own older father stays 18%, and Samuel-1492’s father stays 23%. The actual Faris book has now been inspected, rather than only its catalogue abstract. Printed p.11 uses a dotted possible connection from James of Moneymore to the American brothers; p.12 explicitly reports that evidence for Robert and his brothers’ parentage had not been found. James was the author’s identifiable County Londonderry candidate, not an evidenced father. The retrospective Irish pedigree on pp.8–9 and Samuel’s 1824 Pennsylvania will discussed on p.12 identify an Irish sibling group, including William, James and Robert remaining in Ireland, without joining it to the emigrant brothers. County setting, a compatible generation and the existing family tradition keep James a plausible candidate, but cannot sustain the earlier probable father assessment. See /branches/research-irish-moneymore/#moneymore-probable-father for the source argument. This does not regrade the distinct Corvanaghan identity or older James attachment.

24October2026: the letter-defined Moneymore son’s older James father is now78% probable. This does not upgrade the separate Corvanaghan adult identification or its conditional father edge. /branches/research-irish-moneymore/#irish-four-sons

chapters.title: Four same-name householders
body: The Protestant-householders return lists two James Glasgo and two William Glasgow or Glascy householders in Derryloran.
Repeated forenames make this a useful parish cluster, but do not distinguish fathers, sons, brothers or unrelated men.

chapters.title: A wider parish presence
body: The Derryloran religious return lists two James Glasgo and John at Drumearn, Samuel at Gortein, and William at Killycurry.
It records five definite households across three townlands, while leaving their identities and relationships unstated.

body: James of Corvanaghan, William of a reported Cookstown family, and the Mitchell-family reconstruction are geographically or chronologically relevant leads.

chapters.title: A neighbouring Kildress delegate
body: The original Northern Star report names William Glasgow as a reform delegate at the 16 January Kildress meeting and as its subsequent chairman. William-2915 is old enough and geographically compatible, but the notice names no parents or wife.
Kildress is a neighbouring parish; this occurrence does not identify a Derryloran return householder.

chapters.title: John’s Benjamin and the Drapersfield partners
body: Benjamin-2059’s original 1856 marriage records him as a 20-year-old merchant of Cookstown and his father John as a merchant. This supports the existing father attachment; it does not identify John’s parents or specifically give Killycurragh as Benjamin’s residence.

The 1858 mill case names partners Benjamin and William, another William as their uncle, and the earlier Robert Glasgow and James Woods firm. Robert is father of the singular present plaintiff, without specifying which. A shared uncle does not by itself prove that the partners were brothers.

Benjamin Glasgow of Drapersfield granted land for the July 1870 gathering, after Benjamin-2059’s recorded February death. That current action strongly distinguishes the mill merchant from John’s son. William-3814, a retired bachelor merchant at Loy in 1883, is a strong candidate for the 1856 retirement notice and a possible uncle; the family link still needs a will or deed.
William-1675’s Ohio death notice gives age 55 rather than the attributed Mercury age 56. His 1855 death excludes him as the living 1858 uncle.

proved: Four Derryloran Glasgow households occur in 1740.

The July 1870 Drapersfield Benjamin is strongly distinguished from Benjamin-2059, who died in February.
William-3814 is a strong compatible candidate for the 1856 retired merchant.
hypothesis: Later Cookstown reconstructions may belong to this wider Tyrone setting.
